idea.body: Comparing fractions has two easy shortcuts before any hard work. If two fractions have the same bottom number, the one with the bigger top number is bigger, since more equal-sized parts are being counted. If two fractions have the same top number, the one with the SMALLER bottom number is bigger, since each part is cut bigger. When neither shortcut applies, rewrite both fractions with the same bottom number and compare the top numbers. A faster check is to cross multiply: for a/b and c/d, compare a x d to b x c. A fraction close to 1 whole, like 5/6, beats a fraction close to 0, like 1/6, even before doing any math.

figure.alt: Two bars, each cut into 4 equal pieces: 3 shaded versus 1 shaded shows 3/4 is bigger than 1/4.

steps: Different bottom numbers and different top numbers, so neither shortcut works right away.
Find a common bottom number for both: 18 works, since 6 x 3 is 18 and 9 x 2 is 18.
Rewrite both fractions with bottom 18: 5/6 becomes 15/18, and 7/9 becomes 14/18.
15/18 is bigger than 14/18, so 5/6 is bigger than 7/9.

ways.name: Rewrite with a common denominator
ways.when: Use this when the top and bottom numbers of both fractions are different.
steps: Different bottom numbers and different top numbers, so no shortcut works right away.
Find a common bottom number for both: 18 works, since 6 x 3 is 18 and 9 x 2 is 18.
Rewrite both fractions with bottom 18: 5/6 becomes 15/18, and 7/9 becomes 14/18.
15/18 is bigger than 14/18, so 5/6 is bigger than 7/9.
ways.trap: Comparing the top numbers before the bottom numbers are made to match.

ways.name: Cross multiply
ways.when: Use this when you want a fast check without finding a common denominator.
steps: For a/b and c/d, multiply the top of the first by the bottom of the second: 3 x 7 is 21.
Multiply the top of the second by the bottom of the first: 5 x 4 is 20.
21 is bigger than 20, so the fraction on the same side as 21 is bigger.
3/5 is bigger than 4/7.
ways.trap: Mixing up which cross product belongs to which fraction.

ways.name: Check against one half
ways.when: Use this when one fraction is clearly close to a half and the other is not.
steps: Compare each fraction to one half.
For 3/8: half of 8 is 4, and 3 is less than 4, so 3/8 is less than a half.
For 5/9: half of 9 is 4.5, and 5 is more than 4.5, so 5/9 is more than a half.
A fraction under a half is smaller than one over a half, so 5/9 is bigger.
ways.trap: Assuming the bigger bottom number decides it, without checking against a half.

ways.name: Same top number, smaller bottom wins
ways.when: Use this when both fractions already share the same top number.
steps: Both fractions have the same top number, 3.
The bottom numbers differ: 7 and 4.
A bigger bottom number cuts the whole into smaller pieces, so 3/7 is smaller than 3/4.
3/4 is bigger.
ways.trap: Assuming the bigger bottom number always makes the bigger fraction, forgetting it shrinks each piece.

stretch.prompt: Without finding a common denominator, which is bigger, 17/30 or 19/40? Compare each to 1/2 first.
explanation: Half of 30 is 15, and 17 is more than 15, so 17/30 is past halfway.
Half of 40 is 20, and 19 is less than 20, so 19/40 is under halfway.
A fraction past halfway is always bigger than one under halfway, so 17/30 is bigger.
